1.01.t: Long Bone in Hand — Parts, Physis, Apophysis
1.01.b:
### Hold a long bone → name 4 parts
1) **Diaphysis** → the shaft → thick cortex around the medullary cavity
[[FIG: Fig 1.1, 1.2 · 1.01
2) **Metaphysis** → the flare near the end → thin cortex, cancellous bone, the fastest blood flow
3) **Physis** → the cartilage growth plate → longitudinal growth → closes to a **physeal scar** on X-ray
4) **Epiphysis** → the end beyond the physis → carries the joint surface, built from a **secondary centre**

- Cortical bone ≈ 80% of the skeleton · cancellous ≈ 20% (Netter)
- Metacarpals, metatarsals and phalanges → usually **one physis** each (Netter)
- Thumb metacarpal → physis at the **base** · other metacarpals → at the **head** · phalanges → at the base

### Physis vs apophysis (Nagah p3)
| | Physis | Apophysis |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Growth plate between epiphysis and metaphysis | Bony prominence that takes a tendon or ligament |
| Growth | **Length** of the bone | **No** length → only its own shape |
| Force on it | Compression ("pressure epiphysis") | **Traction** ("traction epiphysis") |
| Examples | Distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius | Greater and lesser trochanter, epicondyles, ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine), AIIS (anterior inferior iliac spine), ischial tuberosity, tibial tuberosity, calcaneal tuberosity, 5th metatarsal base (Handbook) |
| Typical injury | Salter-Harris fracture | **Avulsion** in teenage sport · traction apophysitis |

- Patella → a **sesamoid** bone, not an apophysis
- Osteochondroses → **epiphyseal** (Perthes, Blount, Köhler) vs **apophyseal** (Handbook)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.3, 1.4 · 1.01
- Apophyseal = traction apophysitis → **Osgood-Schlatter** (tibial tuberosity) · **Sever** (calcaneus) · **Sinding-Larsen-Johansson** (lower patellar pole)

PITFALL — "the physis is intra-articular"
- Nagah p3 lists the physis as intra-articular and the apophysis as extra-articular
- Most physes lie **outside** the joint → only the **intracapsular metaphyses** (Section 4) put the physis inside the capsule
- Say → "**physis = length, apophysis = traction; physis inside the joint only where the metaphysis is intracapsular**"

### Periosteum — 2 layers (Nagah p3)
| Layer | Made of | Job |
|---|---|---|
| **Outer fibrous** | Thick collagen → Sharpey fibres anchor tendons | Carries the **periosteal vessels** · attachment |
| **Inner cambium** | Osteoprogenitor cells | **Osteogenic** → appositional growth (**width**) and callus |

- Covers the whole bone **except the articular cartilage** (Bontrager)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.5 · 1.01
- Child → thick, strong, loosely attached → **greenstick fracture** · fast callus · **subperiosteal abscess** (Handbook)
- Adult → thin, firmly attached → pus breaks into soft tissue → **sinus** (Handbook)

CLINICAL PEARL — periosteal hinge (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Supracondylar fracture → periosteum torn on one side, intact on the other = the **hinge** for reduction
- Nerve hurt = on the **torn** side → extension type → anterior tear → AIN (anterior interosseous nerve) or radial
- Flexion type → posterior tear → ulnar nerve
- Repeated manipulation tears the posterior hinge too → **Gartland IV** → unstable in flexion **and** extension

1.02.t: Blood Supply of a Long Bone
1.02.b:
### Four systems (Nagah p4)
| System | Enters | Feeds | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Nutrient** (endosteal) | Nutrient foramen, oblique, mid-shaft | **Inner 2/3** of the cortex + marrow | Main adult supply · high pressure (Handbook) |
| **Periosteal** | Along muscle and fascial attachments | **Outer 1/3** of the cortex | Low pressure · vital in children (Handbook) |
| **Metaphyseal** | Many small holes near the ends | Metaphysis | Joins the nutrient system |
| **Epiphyseal** | Through the capsule, around the physis | Epiphysis + **germinal layer** of the physis | End arteries while the physis is open |

- Nagah lists only nutrient + periosteal → **add metaphyseal and epiphyseal**
  [[FIG: Fig 1.6 · 1.02
- Nutrient foramen points **away from the growing end** → "to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee"
- Normal flow → **centrifugal** (inside → out: nutrient → periosteal)
- Intramedullary reaming → flow turns **centripetal** (periosteum feeds the cortex) → endosteal supply back in ≈3 weeks (Nagah p14)

CLINICAL PEARL — reamed femur, unreamed tibia (Nagah p14)
- Femur → thick muscle cover keeps the periosteal supply → **ream**
- Tibia → thin anteromedial cover, periosteum often stripped by the injury → **unreamed** nail keeps the endosteal supply
- Bonus of reaming → reamings act as graft · periosteal flow and callus rise (Nagah p14)

### Blood & the physis
- **No vessel crosses an open physis** → epiphysis and metaphysis have separate supplies (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.7, 1.8 · 1.02
- Epiphyseal artery dies → the **germinal layer dies → growth stops** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Articular and epiphyseal cartilage → fed by **synovial fluid** → survive ischaemia (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Metaphyseal capillaries make **hairpin loops** → sluggish flow → children's haematogenous osteomyelitis starts in the **metaphysis** (Handbook)

CLINICAL PEARL — why the distal tibia heals badly (Nagah p16)
- **End arteries** with little collateral flow (Prof Baha Karna)
- **Thin soft-tissue cover** → no muscle to bring periosteal vessels
- Poor venous return in the lowest part of the limb

1.03.b:
### Two ways to make bone (Nagah p4)
| | Intramembranous | Endochondral |
|---|---|---|
| Model | No cartilage → bone forms straight in mesenchyme | **Cartilage model** first → replaced by bone |
| Bones | Skull vault, **clavicle** (mostly), flat bones in part | All long bones, vertebrae, pelvis |
| In fracture healing | **Hard callus** (rigid fixation, direct healing) | **Soft callus** (cast, nail → secondary healing) |
| Width or length | **Appositional** growth under the periosteum = width | Physis = **length** |

- Ossification starts ≈ **6th embryonic week**; clavicle first (Bontrager)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.9, 1.10 · 1.03
- **Primary centre** → shaft, before birth · **secondary centre** → epiphysis, mostly after birth
- Distal femur (± proximal tibia) centre → present at birth, term baby (Bontrager) · physes close 20–25 years, **girls earlier**
- Ossification = normal bone formation · calcification = calcium in abnormal tissue (Nagah p4)

### Which physis grows most
- Humerus **80% proximal** · femur **70% distal** · tibia **55% proximal** (Campbell Fig 38.4)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.11 · 1.03
- Rule → "**toward the knee, away from the elbow**" → physeal injury at the shoulder, wrist or knee costs most length

### Zones of the growth plate → epiphysis to metaphysis
| Zone | Cells | Job | Disease in this zone |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reserve / germinal** | Few, scattered, beside the epiphysis | Stem cells · stores matrix | Damaged by epiphyseal **ischaemia** → arrest |
| **Proliferative** | Flat cells in **columns** | **Length** comes from here | **Achondroplasia** (Netter) |
| **Hypertrophic** → maturation · degeneration · **provisional calcification** | Cells swell 5–10× (Netter) · little matrix | Prepare cartilage for bone | **Fractures** · SCFE (slipped capital femoral epiphysis) · rickets (widened plate) |
| **Metaphysis** → primary then secondary spongiosa | Vessels invade · osteoblasts | Woven → lamellar bone | Osteomyelitis |

- Mnemonic from the epiphysis → "**R-P-H-M**: Rest, Proliferate, Hypertrophy, Make bone"
  [[FIG: Fig 1.12, 1.13 · 1.03
- **Groove of Ranvier** → physis grows **wider** · **ring of LaCroix** → fibrous ring holding its edge (Netter)
- Normal physis ≈ **2 mm** thick · rickets ≈ **5 mm** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Child → ligament stronger than physis → the **physis fails before the ligament** (Netter)

PITFALL — which zone fails?
- Classic + Nagah p18 + Prof Abdel-Ghani → **hypertrophic zone, at the provisional calcification layer** (least matrix, before mineral)
- Campbell 15th → "the proliferative zone, the weakest region"
- Say → "**hypertrophic zone, at provisional calcification** → germinal layer stays with the epiphysis → growth goes on"

### Physis on X-ray
- **Salter-Harris II** → metaphyseal spike = **Thurston-Holland** fragment (Campbell)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.14 · 1.03
- Salter-Harris III–IV → cross the germinal layer + joint → open reduction (Campbell)
- **Harris (Park) lines** → parallel = growth resumed · tilted = **partial arrest** (bar) · none = complete arrest (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

1.04.t: Intracapsular Metaphysis — Why Osteomyelitis Becomes Septic Arthritis
1.04.b:
### The 4 joints (Nagah p7)
| Joint | Intracapsular metaphysis |
|---|---|
| **Hip** | Proximal femoral neck |
| **Shoulder** | Proximal humeral metaphysis |
| **Elbow** | Radial neck |
| **Ankle** | Distal fibula (lateral malleolus) |

- Mnemonic → "**HSEA**: Hip, Shoulder, Elbow, Ankle" · the **knee has none**
  [[FIG: Fig 1.15 · 1.04

### Four routes to septic arthritis (Nagah p7)
1) **Infant** → vessels still cross the physis → metaphysis → epiphysis → joint
2) **Intracapsular metaphysis** → abscess opens inside the capsule
3) A structure runs from the metaphysis into the joint → **long head of biceps**
4) **Septicaemia** → seeds the synovium directly

- After the vessels stop crossing → the physis is a **barrier** to the abscess (Campbell)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.16 · 1.04

CLINICAL PEARL — septic hip in an infant (Campbell)
- Shared vessels across the physis (Campbell Fig 24.1) → metaphysis, epiphysis and joint infected **at once**
- Pus under pressure → **femoral head destroyed** → drain as an emergency

PITFALL — up to what age do vessels cross the physis?
- Campbell ch 24 → under **18 months**; Campbell ch 23 → under **2 years**
- Say → "**transphyseal vessels until about 18 months to 2 years**"

### Three structural types
| Type | Sub-type | Movement | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fibrous** | Suture | None | Skull |
| | Syndesmosis | Slight | **Distal tibiofibular**, interosseous membrane |
| | Gomphosis | None | Tooth in its socket |
| **Cartilaginous** | **Primary** = synchondrosis (hyaline, temporary) | None | **Physis**, triradiate cartilage, C2 subdental synchondrosis |
| | **Secondary** = symphysis (fibrocartilage, midline) | Slight | **Pubic symphysis**, intervertebral disc, manubriosternal |
| **Synovial** | 7 shapes (next table) | Free | Most limb joints |

- Function names → **synarthrosis** (none) · **amphiarthrosis** (slight) · **diarthrosis** (free) (Bontrager)
  [[FIG: Fig 1.17, 1.18 · 1.05
- Primary cartilaginous joints **ossify**; secondary ones **stay** for life
- Synovial joint = cartilage + subchondral bone + capsule + **synovium** (makes the fluid that feeds the cartilage) (Netter)

### Synovial joints — 7 shapes
| Shape | Axes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Plane | Gliding | Intercarpal, acromioclavicular, facet joints |
| Hinge (ginglymus) | 1 | Interphalangeal, humero-ulnar |
| Pivot (trochoid) | 1 | Proximal + distal radio-ulnar, atlanto-axial (dens) |
| Condylar / ellipsoid | 2 | Wrist (radiocarpal), MCP (metacarpophalangeal), MTP (metatarsophalangeal) |
| **Saddle** (sellar) | 2 | **Thumb CMC** (carpometacarpal), sternoclavicular, calcaneocuboid |
| Ball & socket | 3 | **Hip**, shoulder |
| Bicondylar | 2 | **Knee**, temporomandibular |

- Mnemonic → "**Please Help Pick Cool Socks By Bicycle**" → Plane, Hinge, Pivot, Condylar, Saddle, Ball, Bicondylar
  [[FIG: Fig 1.19, 1.20, 1.21, 1.22, 1.23 · 1.05
- Deep socket → stable, less motion (hip) · shallow socket → mobile, less stable (shoulder)

PITFALL — knee and ankle shape
- Knee → "bicondylar" (Bontrager) vs "modified hinge / trochoginglymus" (Sobotta)
- Ankle → "hinge" (Sobotta) vs "saddle" (Bontrager)
- Say → "**knee = modified hinge (bicondylar) with rotation; ankle = hinge**"

- Three by tissue → **fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial**

- The nerve to a joint also supplies the **muscles that move it** and the **skin over their insertions**

- Hip → femoral, obturator, sciatic, nerve to quadratus femoris → the same nerves reach the knee
